title: Integral lower-degree commutator of nonopposite Chevalley divided powers
statement: Let $\mathfrak g$ be a finite-dimensional split semisimple Lie algebra over $\mathbf Q$ [def-wf-lie-algebra], [def-wf-semisimple-lie-algebra], with splitting Cartan subalgebra $\mathfrak h$ and reduced crystallographic root system $R\subset\mathfrak h^\vee$. Fix a Chevalley basis: $h_i$ are the simple coroots, the $e_\gamma$ are nonzero root vectors ($[h,e_\gamma]=\gamma(h)e_\gamma$ for $h\in\mathfrak h$), $[e_\gamma,e_{-\gamma}]=h_\gamma$, where $h_\gamma\in\mathfrak h$ is the coroot of $\gamma$, the element of $[\mathfrak g_\gamma,\mathfrak g_{-\gamma}]$ with $\gamma(h_\gamma)=2$ for the root spaces $\mathfrak g_{\pm\gamma}=\{x\in\mathfrak g:[h,x]=\pm\gamma(h)x\text{ for all }h\in\mathfrak h\}$, and for $\gamma+\delta\in R$ one has $[e_\gamma,e_\delta]=\pm(p_{\gamma,\delta}+1)e_{\gamma+\delta}$, where $p_{\gamma,\delta}=\max\{p\ge0:\delta-p\gamma\in R\}$; the bracket is zero if the sum is neither a root nor zero. Set $U=T_{\mathbf Q}(\mathfrak g)/(x\otimes y-y\otimes x-[x,y])$ and $e_\gamma^{(a)}=e_\gamma^a/a!$. For distinct roots $\alpha,\beta$ with $\alpha\ne-\beta$ and integers $m,n\ge0$, the difference $$e_\alpha^{(m)}e_\beta^{(n)}-e_\beta^{(n)}e_\alpha^{(m)}$$ is a finite integer linear combination of words $e_{\gamma_1}^{(a_1)}\cdots e_{\gamma_s}^{(a_s)}$ with $a_j\ge1$, $\sum_j a_j<m+n$, and $\gamma_j\in R\cap(\mathbf Z_{\ge0}\alpha+\mathbf Z_{\ge0}\beta)$. Each word can be taken to have weight $\sum_j a_j\gamma_j=m\alpha+n\beta$. If $m=0$ or $n=0$ the difference is zero.

proof.text: If $m=0$ or $n=0$, the difference is zero because $e_\gamma^{(0)}=1$, represented by the empty linear combination. Otherwise apply [lem-sfb-chevalley-string-central-parity] to the given pair. Use its ordering $(a,b)$ and put $(M,N)=(m,n)$ if $(a,b)=(\alpha,\beta)$, or $(M,N)=(n,m)$ otherwise. The original commutator is respectively the resulting commutator or its negative. The cone, weight and degree requirements are invariant under this interchange. Use the integers $q,c_k,z_d$ and elements $Y_k,C_d$ supplied by that node. Their identities also hold in $U$, since the defining relations give $xy-yx=[x,y]$.

source.place: Agent coefficient argument for the supporting divided-power identity; Theorem 23.71, pp.508--509, for the assumed bracket normalization. The two non-elementary inputs are separately stated nodes.

proof.text:
Work coefficientwise in $U[[s,t]]$, with central variables. Define $E_\gamma(w)=\sum_{j\geq0}w^j e_\gamma^j/j!$ when $w$ has zero constant term. The binomial expansion of repeated commutators gives
$$(\operatorname{ad}x)^k(y)=\sum_{i=0}^k(-1)^i\binom{k}{i}x^{k-i}yx^i.$$
Indeed apply $[x,-]$ and use Pascal's identity for the inductive step, starting at $k=0$. Thus multiplying the two exponential series gives
$$E_a(s)e_bE_a(-s)=\sum_{k=0}^q s^kY_k.$$
Also $E_a(s)E_a(-s)=1$, since its coefficient in positive degree $k$ is $e_a^k(1-1)^k/k!$. Conjugation by these inverse series preserves products; expand the exponential in powers of $t$ to obtain
$$E_a(s)E_b(t)=\exp\!\left(t\sum_{k=0}^q s^kY_k\right)E_a(s).$$
All operations have finite coefficient sums; no analytic convergence or nilpotence of $e_a$ in $U$ is asserted.

source.place: Agent coefficient argument for the supporting divided-power identity; Theorem 23.71, pp.508--509, for the assumed bracket normalization. The two non-elementary inputs are separately stated nodes.

proof.text:
Apply [lem-sfb-formal-class-two-exponential] in $A=U$ to $Z_{k+1}=ts^kY_k$ for $0\leq k\leq q$. These series have zero constant coefficient, and their triple brackets vanish by [lem-sfb-chevalley-string-central-parity]. Its integers give
$$E_a(s)E_b(t)=E_b(t)\left(\prod_{k=1}^q E_{b+ka}(c_k s^kt)\right)\left(\prod_{\substack{1\leq d\leq2q\\2b+da\in R}}E_{2b+da}(-z_d s^dt^2)\right)E_a(s).$$
The first product is in increasing $k$, the second in increasing $d$. To justify splitting the correction exponential, note that each $[Y_i,Y_j]$ commutes with each $Y_k$; hence it commutes with each product $Y_kY_l$ and so with each $[Y_k,Y_l]$. Thus the $C_d$ commute mutually. Apply the same formal factorization lemma to the correction summands, whose brackets are now zero. Terms with $C_d=0$ contribute one.

source.place: Agent coefficient argument for the supporting divided-power identity; Theorem 23.71, pp.508--509, for the assumed bracket normalization. The two non-elementary inputs are separately stated nodes.

proof.text:
Take the coefficient of $s^Mt^N$ in this finite product of formal series. Assign exponent $u$ to the first factor, $v$ to the last, $A_k$ to the $k$th string factor and $B_d$ to the $d$th correction factor. Every coefficient is the corresponding ordered word of divided powers multiplied by the integer $\prod_k c_k^{A_k}\prod_d(-z_d)^{B_d}$. Its indices satisfy
$$M=v+\sum_k kA_k+\sum_d dB_d,\qquad N=u+\sum_k A_k+2\sum_d B_d.$$
There are finitely many such nonnegative indices. The unique contribution with all $A_k=B_d=0$ is $e_b^{(N)}e_a^{(M)}$; subtract it. For every remaining contribution the divided-power degree $D=u+v+\sum_k A_k+\sum_d B_d$ satisfies
$$M+N-D=\sum_k kA_k+\sum_d(d+1)B_d>0.$$
Its weight is $ub+va+\sum_k A_k(b+ka)+\sum_d B_d(2b+da)=Ma+Nb$. All roots used belong to $R\cap(\mathbf Z_{\geq0}a+\mathbf Z_{\geq0}b)$. Omit exponent-zero factors, combine identical words by adding integer coefficients, and restore the ordering and sign from step 1. This proves all clauses.
